column2: On his arrival, Cage gives a preliminary speech denouncing Beethoven's harmonic tradition in favor of rhythm and duration in Satie, then performs only Satie throughout his stay, exasperating the German émigrés, Albers among them. Words: A speech against Beethoven, for Satie Atmosphere: Unease and irritation among the German exiles, Cage's deliberate provocation Stakes: A conflict over musical heritage and cultural authority at the college

A performance of Satie's “The Ruse of Medusa”: the student Arthur Penn directs; Fuller plays Baron Medusa, Elaine de Kooning his daughter Frisette, Cunningham the “costly mechanical monkey”; sets by the de Koonings; absurd monologues, stylized non-naturalistic acting, no separation between audience and stage. Photos by Clemens Kalischer. Words: Satie's absurd monologues Atmosphere: Absurd buffoonery, playful avant-garde Stakes: Rehabilitating Cage at the college; a milestone on the way to the 1952 Happening

Fuller builds moving forms with bobby pins and clothespins, folds an icosahedron into a tetrahedron, unrolls a history of calculation punished by death in the Middle Ages, extols the numbers 3 and 9, draws a square on the blackboard, traces the diagonal, and greets it affectionately. Words: Ah... here is “our old friend, the hypotenuse” Atmosphere: Dazzling, dizzying, spectacular Stakes: A man converts a room to the geometric universe

After nighttime calculations, on a damp morning, the framework of blind slats is assembled; the 22-foot dome refuses to rise; it is good-humoredly christened the “Supine Dome”; Fuller claims he wanted it so, to demonstrate progressive reinforcement. Words: Fuller: “you succeed when you stop failing”; it is like confetti, so light it cannot hurt anyone Atmosphere: Damp, collective, good-natured despite the failure Stakes: Failure embraced as teaching

As soon as he arrives in the summer of 1948, Bill de Kooning gives a lecture on Cézanne and the color of Veronese; Albers's devotees flee his classes, leaving the field open to a few romantics such as Passlof. Words: Pat Passlof: as soon as he arrived, Bill gave a lecture titled “Cézanne and the Color of Veronese” Atmosphere: A Dionysian riposte to the reigning Apollonian spirit Stakes: A clash of two conceptions of art within the same college

In Albers's room, the students, seated at desks, cautiously work on small, neat compositions that are critiqued collectively. In Bill's, standing at easels, they boldly paint large canvases and wait for the master's individual visit, who opens the dialogue only once their problems have appeared on the canvas. Atmosphere: the contrast between Albers's precise discipline and Bill's free daring Stakes: two conceptions of art face to face, which the students pass through in turn
Beaumont Newhall photographs Elaine de Kooning attending Buckminster Fuller's class.

Alone in her studio, she rereads the diary page on which she has just written her feelings, tears it up, cuts out the words, and reassembles them into a disordered, illegible pattern; she titles the whole Secrets. Atmosphere: intimacy, concealment, a mental jigsaw Stakes: words enter her art; the first scene of the need to hide

Every spot of paint spilled on the rug was offset by the same color in the corresponding positions of the other three quadrants, so that the symmetrical spots seemed part of the rug Atmosphere: The knowing games of young artists Stakes: The root of Weil's sense of symmetry and balance

The man wonders aloud (direct action? saying what is? elementary desire?), looks for Henry Faust, flies into a mad rage at being kept incommunicado, calls the beast stupid and mute, and beats it with his fists; the elephant tramples him and kicks him out of the enclosure. Words: He tells the stupid, harmless beast to speak to him; is he still cut off from all communication? It has become as enormous and silent as an elephant. Atmosphere: the grayness of the zoo, solitary exasperation Stakes: the failure of communication reduced to violence; immediate punishment

Piet Duyck comes in from the dunes, sand in his hair and eyelashes, saliva on his chin, in tears; he has seen a vision or dreamed it. The father of Joan, the child at his left arm, silently puts his right arm around his shoulders. Harry Tyler refuses to ask what is wrong — if Piet Duyck is crying, it is serious beyond all remedy — and wipes his face and brushes the sand from his hair, making him close his eyes. With his eyes closed, Mynheer sees only darkness: it is from this total eclipse that the vision came back. Words: Tyler: he will not ask him what is wrong, friend… he will have to go on crying to the end, there is no help for it; close your eyes. Atmosphere: adult grief, a child solemn and mute with respect and curiosity, the sailor's practical tenderness Stakes: a grief of a cosmic order received with a gesture of washing

Mynheer, a shining mirror in hand like Perseus, prescribes: the country, statistics in support, and a human community to be invented to satisfy the few simple needs. Lothair exclaims, Again?, he who invented utopias as a diversion. Mynheer first asks whether they have intercourse; Emily says no; a lesson in raw evidence. Lothair, bitter, speaks of a flesh trembling in a vise — his powerful hand, for its part, does not tremble. Duyck looks the two Gorgons in the face, his heart turns to stone, he staggers, they ask after his health: he draws from his breast a handful of stone — a cornerstone for building a good city. Words: “It's necessary to fuck if you want to have children.” — “It doesn't exist but we can invent that.” — “A cornerstone for building a good city.” Atmosphere: bitter, prophetic comedy, modesty overstepped Stakes: founding a community on a sterile couple and a heart of stone

Lothair objects that community does not exist; Mynheer: one can invent it. Without beating about the bush he asks the couple whether they fuck; no — so they touch on something right away: one must fuck to have children; Lothair answers bitterly that his flesh is caught in a death grip and holds out his powerful hand, which does not tremble. Words: “It doesn't exist but we can invent that”; “It's necessary to fuck if you want to have children” Atmosphere: the brutality of a medical examination mixed with fable Stakes: the invention of community begins with the most intimate question

Duyck looks the two Gorgons in the face, his heart turns to stone, he staggers; the others solicitously ask whether he is ill; he draws from his chest a small handful of stone: “a cornerstone for building a good city”. Words: “A cornerstone for building a good city” Atmosphere: a metaphysical fable, the anxious tenderness of those present Stakes: the personal price of lucidity

Mynheer sets out the rite of Remus and asks who will be killed and plowed into the field; silence, looks that size one another up; he licks his lips and raises the heart-stone; all draw back, shouting, except his son, who challenges him; Horatio bursts into sobs and howls; Minetta turns the threat into a promise of benevolent haunting; laughter with bared teeth. Words: Horatio: “I'm not yet at the point to say 'Let me die rather!' But from this moment on I do not intend to stop wailing”; Minetta: “you can't get rid of me now. Won't I haunt that city of yours?” Atmosphere: violet to black, contained panic, nervous giggles Stakes: must there be a death for the community to exist?

To relieve the founders' anguish, Harry Tyler tells a joke: two displaced persons tell each other their destinations, London and Paris; the third: South Africa! — so far? — “so far from where?” Words: “So far?” — “So far from where?” Atmosphere: the dark laughter of people with no place of origin Stakes: exile as the founders' condition

A tall, nameless redhead introduces himself as the Stranger of the scheme, practices his role, changes masks every other day (his red hair can be seen beneath them), denies being a Jew, reels off his arithmetic of interlaced fingers (22, 33, 55, 66); in the evening, drunk, he insults the community seekers, cowards before death, and refuses to leave. Words: “Me? I'm going to South Africa!”; “Hell, I'll go away! Can you make me?” Atmosphere: daytime grotesque turning sinister at dusk Stakes: the role the community requires overflows it and threatens it

In the dark, a flashlight lights up one face after another; a bell rings; each reels off his hatred — of children, of unsatisfied sex, of interrupted sleep, of importunate friends, of poor clothes, of those who crunch apples too loudly, of those who give beatings, of the order of things; the narrator adds his hatred of the poetic art that has cost him his life; the twelfth stroke: an invocation of the Creator Spirit. Words: “I hate the order of things that could, it seems, so easily have given me happiness, because my wants are simple”; “I hate you who eat apples loudly” Atmosphere: darkness, jutting jaws, a furious bell, collective catharsis Stakes: the community is born only from the avowal of the hatred it was meant to allow

In the fall of 1948, Elaine reads Kierkegaard to Bill and observes the affinity between the painter's stubbornness and the philosopher's exaltation of it, as well as the appeal of ordinary heroes. Words: Elaine notes an affinity between the two in Bill's stubbornness and K.'s exaltation of it Atmosphere: Domestic and intellectual, the couple's complicity Stakes: The painter finds in Kierkegaard a kindred spirit and a confirmation of his own labor

Fuller tries to assemble his first geodesic dome during the summer; the assembly fails; he recovers thanks to the student Snelson's tensegrity innovations. Atmosphere: Summer, a building site for experiment Stakes: Failure embraced as method in Fuller

The end of scene 2: Baron Medusa, sounding like a Groucho Marx twenty years ahead of his time, dismisses Astolfo, Frisette's fiancé Words: “Get out now!... Off like a gun!... Come back in ten minutes... I shan't be here.” Atmosphere: Pre-Marx Brothers slapstick, ribald verbal vaudeville, burlesque sight gags Stakes: The deliberate breaking of the fourth wall and the destruction of narrative continuity

The faculty exhausts a list of candidates who are too busy; the Harvard architect Bertrand Goldberg, a former Bauhaus member, declines; Albers falls back on Fuller, who then carries a heavy record of failures Atmosphere: Last-minute improvisation Stakes: The chance of who was available sets a major transformation of the college in motion

Every morning, the three men have breakfast under the trees and laughingly invent a traveling caravan school that would abolish all conventional approaches to school. Words: Fuller: they spent the summer “on a fun schematic new school”; “We would finish anything”; the caravan would go “from city to city”. Atmosphere: Joyful, knowing, early-morning, open-air. Stakes: The birth of an anti-Albers front of radical experimentation.

In a largely Germanic school, Cage devotes the whole summer to Satie, which irritates. Albers requires a talk before each concert; the first ones go well. In midsession, Cage gives a lecture longer than the others in which he denounces Beethoven in order to set out Satie's views. Words: Cage: the lecture had the effect of a bomb falling on the place Atmosphere: Scandal in an audience steeped in German culture Stakes: A symbolic clash between Albers's Germanic heritage and the French avant-garde embodied by Satie

Overwhelmed by the Giacometti exhibition, Bill leaves the gallery, walks around the block to calm down, then comes back to study the work more closely. Atmosphere: Vertigo before a work that seems the output of a civilization. Stakes: Showing the physical effect of art on artists.

Pollock, probably drunk, reels off his unpleasant opinions of Gorky's painting. Gorky smiles dangerously, pulls a pencil from one pocket and a penknife from the other, and, without taking his eyes off Jackson's face, slowly sharpens the lead to an inch-long point. Pollock studies the face and the point by turns, flinches a little, then gives a sly, approving little smile, turns on his heel, and walks away, satisfied. Words: Gorky, honeyed: “Pardon me, Mr. Pollock, you and I are different kinds of artists” Atmosphere: Contained, theatrical violence, at once threat and caress Stakes: Who dominates whom in the rivalry of the Abstract Expressionists

A laundry basket tied to the sled with both children in it; Ann pushes, loses control, the sled tips into a ditch; a dash to the infirmary; Frances strokes the nurse's beard during the stitching Atmosphere: maternal panic, calmed by the stroking of the beard

Sawyer argues for art as an intellectual enterprise and for the creation of the Division of Arts, and invites alumni to enjoy the original art of their time; he evokes laboratories of the arts with woodworking shops, studios, darkrooms, and presses — a vague intimation of a Bauhaus-Black Mountain-style foundation course at Yale College. A quotation: “candor compels us to conclude...” about the alumni's visual adolescence; President Charles Seymour Jr. inspired the division.

On February 6, 1948, Sawyer writes to the chairman of the university committee: “Frankly I'm not impressed” by the alumni proposed; six days later he invites Albers. The University Council created in early 1948: 25 alumni appointed by the Yale Corporation
After seeing the photographs of Martha's Vineyard and Gloucester at the Charles Egan gallery, Albers organizes an exhibition of Siskind's recent work at the college.

As the opening of the first exhibition approaches, Willem, Elaine, and Charles Egan settle on the final titles of the paintings in the course of an evening. Atmosphere: Last-minute improvisation, the night before the opening. Stakes: The name against the undecidable — echoing his distrust of overly neat titles.
Elaine takes part in a panel at the Club alongside O'Hara, Goldberg, Hartigan, Resnick, and Mitchell.

A few years after the late 1950s, Elaine asks Sandler why none of the Club's two hundred members is Black; Sandler replies that there were only a handful of Black artists in the downtown art world. 200 members of the Club Consequences: One of the few voices to raise the question

A decade after Black Mountain, Cage dedicates to Elaine a work in which the I Ching determines by chance the arrangement of the notational techniques, a transmutation of musical notation into an abstract visual language. The pianist may play the elements in any order

A new payment on the original mortgage; a debt of $10,000 (improvements) moves into first position, repayable at $1,000 a year for ten years; the second mortgage ($16,500, held by the Dreier family, in the form of demand notes) remains. The banks refuse to refinance (an annual deficit, reluctance toward religious and educational institutions). Stephen Forbes lends $9,500 to stagger the two mortgages. $10,000 in first mortgage; $16,500 in second; a Forbes loan of $9,500. Consequences: The college survives thanks to the loan, tuition, and gifts.
Kazin and Hannah Arendt warmly recommend Rosenfeld to Levi (letters of April 12 and 13, 1948); Rosenfeld writes to Levi on March 18 and April 15. Consequences: Rosenfeld recruited

Cunningham visits Black Mountain for the first time with John Cage in April 1948; he will return five times to teach and perform, on stays ranging from a few days to six weeks. Stays of several days to six weeks; five later visits. Consequences: The start of a lasting relationship that will culminate in the founding of his company there.
Cage arrives at the college without a teaching post: he is Cunningham's piano accompanist. Consequences: A visibility that leads Albers to offer him a post for the summer session

Gathered before the opening, they look for a title for each painting; the rule: three votes in favor required Atmosphere: A democratic ritual taming the “unfinished” work Stakes: Pinning down the elusive before the exhibition

During a conversation on the porch, a man sits down and takes part in the talk for hours before an attendant from a nearby psychiatric hospital comes to claim him. Cunningham is delighted to see how well he had fitted in. Words: Cunningham: they had got along well… the mad do not need to be locked up — their perspective can contribute a great deal to society. Atmosphere: Unusual, relaxed, as if everything seemed perfectly normal. Stakes: Revealing the community's radical openness, able to welcome even madness.

Nell Rice, gazing at the trees in the distance, makes her elegant remark, which charms Cunningham. Words: she has been contemplating this landscape for twenty years and has concluded that only one tree is out of place. Atmosphere: Witty, deadpan. Stakes: Sketching the culture of looking peculiar to Black Mountain.

Cage plays sixteen sonatas and four interludes for prepared piano, then, faced with astonished but friendly questions, sets out his conception at length: time rather than harmony, art as integration, the society to come. Words: it begins with music and ends with a common human nature. Atmosphere: Rather dizzying for the community: just comprehensible enough for it to recognize its own concerns, vague enough for each person to fill in the blanks. Stakes: A genuine meeting of minds, a prelude to the Black Mountain of the 1950s.

After the Gorky affair (an anonymous reviewer having written that Gorky was influenced by Bill, which revolted him and Elaine, suspected of being the author), she gets the reviews signed with initials; her first signed review is on the late landscapes of Friedman, a postal employee who had died two years earlier a limit of 200 words per review; a fee of two dollars per review; the average hourly manufacturing wage: $1.32; Fairfield Porter estimates the reviewers' earnings at five cents an hour Consequences: the birth of a major voice in twentieth-century art criticism

A letter from his mother in early May announces the sudden death from a heart attack of his older brother, twenty. A glorious, sunny day, white clouds over the pines, the red clay road, the still lake; a small auburn dog (Red? Jake?) keeps him company in his grief on the path from the Studies Building to the dormitory. A thought that marks him forever: what is the use of anything? a twenty-year-old brother; a reddish clay road; a small auburn dog Consequences: He is not sure he has ever got over it

Cunningham writes to the Alberses on May 17, 1948, Lippold to Albers on May 24, and Cage sends a night letter to Dreier and Albers on June 17, preparing their arrival. night letter of June 17, 1948 Consequences: The arrival of the Cage/Cunningham/Lippold trio in the summer of 1948

She enthusiastically sends Whitehead's book The Function of Reason (1929) to Ted Dreier for his birthday, in May 1948. The book: Alfred North Whitehead, The Function of Reason, 1929. Consequences: A trace of Whitehead's influence on the BMC circle.

Early May, a letter from his mother: his older brother, twenty, dead of a heart attack; he walks from the Studies Building to the dormitory under a glorious sky, puffy clouds over the pines, the red clay road, the still lake; a small auburn dog keeps him company Words: An invasive thought: what is the use of anything? Atmosphere: mourning beneath a dazzling beauty of the world; a heartrending contrast Stakes: the most poignant moment of his stay; has he got over it? He is not sure
For Dreier's birthday, Anni enthusiastically sends him Whitehead's The Function of Reason (1929). Stakes: Sharing a thought on event and becoming with a founding colleague.

A night departure in torrential rain; refusing to rent pillows at fifty cents, unable to sleep, they read detective magazines; in the morning, the train climbs the mountain before a brilliant green landscape. 2 round-trip train tickets; pillows rented at $0.50; Bill's pay: $200 for two months

A dismal first impression: isolated students lounging on the grass, looking strangely apathetic and forlorn; relief at being welcomed by Albers like old friends. A cottage furnished to the minimum: a table, two chairs, a bed, a chest of drawers

After seeing the floors of tiny identical studios in the Studies Building, Bill chooses to paint in the cottage's living room; Elaine takes a studio, palette set on the desk, a view of Lake Eden through the window. A studio: room for a desk, a chair, and a cot; Elaine paints on sheets of wrapping paper nailed to the wall

Elaine, quick and impetuous, tries to solve several visual problems in a single composition; Albers tears up her work, judging her approach too extravagant. About thirty students in the class, including Ruth Asawa, Hazel Larsen, Pat Passlof Consequences: Decades later, she will contrast Albers's method with Bill's patient teaching

Elaine, at first disappointed by Fuller's stiff appearance, is won over by his whirlwind lecture on ecology, engineering, and technology, with geometric constructions of clothespins, and enrolls in his course; she is the only woman, the others being mostly architecture and engineering students from Harvard. At the blackboard, Fuller draws a square and its diagonal and exclaims: ah, here is “our old friend, the hypotenuse” Consequences: Takes part in building the dome

Fuller builds increasingly complex three-dimensional forms with the table silverware, helped by Elaine's bobby pins, discussing their mechanical properties; when Elaine's order arrives, she does not want to take back her utensils and grabs a clip from her bag to hold her hamburger. Fuller's rejoinder: which brings us to the paradox of tensile strength!

According to Elaine's recollection, the 1948 summer session brings together seventy-four students, from teenagers to veterans of the Second World War; each pays 350 dollars for the summer and must take part in the chores. 74 students; 350 dollars per person; compulsory chores

Peter Grippe and his wife Florence report that Bill slept in a dormitory; Lieber notes that before the fast-food era, Americans often ate hamburgers with a knife and fork in restaurants, as Bill did, in the European manner. A dormitory; a hamburger eaten with knife and fork

The Erik Satie play performed in the summer of 1948 was translated by Mary Caroline Richards, a teacher of literature and writing married to another faculty member; in the original French production, the role of Frisette was played by Madeleine Milhaud, wife of the composer Darius Milhaud, an actress.

After six years with interruptions, she graduates in June 1948 with a paper signed by the chairman of the music department at Columbia University, her outside examiner; happy and relieved, she stays for that summer's Music and Art Institute. the signer: the chairman of Columbia's music department Consequences: The summer of 1948 with Cage.

At the end of June, in high spirits, they pack brushes, paints, pads, jeans, bathing suits, a good suit for Bill and two dresses for Elaine, and take the night train. Luggage: brushes, paints, notebooks, jeans, bathing suits, a suit, two dresses

At the end of June, in high spirits, they pack brushes, paints, pads, jeans, bathing suits, a good suit for Bill, two dresses for Elaine. The porter rents pillows at 50 cents apiece; they refuse to save money, regret it all night, and read detective novels until dawn

A stooped student with long hair and glasses drives them in an old station wagon. A first glimpse of the campus: Faulknerian desolation, isolated, sullen students on the grass. Bill: an urge to leave again. Albers's warm welcome puts them back on their feet. “Ach so! The de Koonings!” — Albers embraces them like old friends

The cottage: bare wooden floors, one large room with a table and chairs, a bedroom. A tour: Albers describes the raising of each building; the Quiet House, a wooden meditation house built in memory of Ted Dreier's son, killed in a car accident. A long building with two floors of tiny studios on a Bauhaus design. Bill refuses the small studios and chooses the living room; Elaine pushes her desk to the window and paints on kraft paper nailed to the wall, facing the lake; a dock in the distance with bathers

Albers explains the food system: no choice, everyone eats the same thing, no waste. The dish of the day: a salad of sausages and bananas. Bill: “Looks like something Elaine would make,” a mutual compliment with Albers. Bill eats two bowls of soup first so as to treat the salad as dessert. Meals announced by a resounding bell; a meeting at 6 p.m.

Sitting on the dock, they laughingly ignore the bell (Elaine: “Pavlov's dogs”), arrive 20 minutes later, and find the hall empty: every scrap has disappeared. From then on they sprint at the sound of the bell. Consequences: Never again late for a meal
Some faculty members absent from the party — a second sign of the open and veiled hostilities that form an oppressive undercurrent all summer.
Elaine effortlessly remembers all their names, she who kept forgetting those of the faculty.

74 summer students (about half of them new). Guests: Peter Grippe (sculpture), Richard Lischer (woodworking), Winslow Ames (history of prints in July, director of the art museum in Springfield, Missouri), Beaumont Newhall (3rd summer, finishing his History of Photography), Charles Burchard (architecture in August, Harvard School of Design), Erwin Bodky (pianist and harpsichordist, The Development of Keyboard Music and The Beethoven Sonatas — the source of a notable tangle with Cage), Edgar Kaufman Jr. (industrial design, MoMA), Isaac Rosenfeld (Tolstoy and “creative writing,” who, according to Kazin, despised Black Mountain). Albers teaches Color and Design; Anni Albers and Trude Guermonprez weaving. 74 students; pay: room and board, $100 for travel expenses, $25 per week of attendance

Droll, out of the Valley Forge Military Academy after two years at Michigan State College, arrives at the end of June among some forty new students and suffers an immediate shock: he has never heard of Cage, Cunningham, de Kooning, or Fuller, and has never seen so many young people in jeans, khaki trousers cut off at the knee, dyed shirts, sandals, even beards. 19; loyal, trustworthy, and cooperative, according to the head of the military academy; sport jackets with matching ties Consequences: A personal transformation; he decides to stay on as a full-time student the following year

Beneath the summer's sparkling surface, a critical confrontation is brewing between Albers and Dreier on one side and Levi and Rondthaler on the other. The summer people know almost nothing of it — except Fuller, who is aware of it because Dreier confides in him. Consequences: A crisis ahead for the community

Fuller, always short of materials for his structures and his classes, goes to Asheville to get them; de Kooning likes to go along to talk philosophy. Fuller: Bill is a really, really marvelous thinker. Car trips between Asheville and the campus

Fuller sleeps in two-hour naps every six hours and spends much of the rest of the time talking: theories about everything — removing the walls of buildings, the differences between inland cultures and water cultures, stacking hundreds of houses in airplanes to drop them on disadvantaged regions. 2 hours of sleep every 6 hours

Lectures of four to five hours; halfway through, Fuller calls a little intermission, opens the curtains behind him, and, while the others smoke and talk, brings out tables covered with geometric figures — Fuller and his magic show. Elaine de Kooning is said to have fallen in love with Bucky at the moment he said: “And here's our old friend, the tetrahedron.” Tables of geometric figures; curtains

Cunningham's only solo concert for the community in 1948, assisted by Louise Lippold (a former student) and Sara Hamill (a current student). The audience, ignorant of modern dance, cannot measure the radical nature of his break — like children delighted by a Klee for not knowing that portraits are supposed to look like Rembrandts. What they see: an orderly discipline and a concern for the development of the person in an individual way.

Charged with a course on the structure of music and choreography and with concerts of modern music, Cage devotes the entire series, apart from a single concert of his own works, to Erik Satie — culminating in Satie's play Le Piège de Méduse (the sentence is cut off by the footnote reference). A single concert of works by Cage Consequences: Tension foreshadowed with Bodky and with the college's established musical taste

Just before the summer institute begins, the Board of Fellows balks at Levi's proposals: to hire new teachers and enlarge the Board by electing new members. The Board also refuses to authorize a trip by the Levis to Chicago to recruit. On one of the points, the Levi camp wins by one vote, but during a recess, with some of Levi's supporters out of the room, the vote is reconsidered and reversed. Levi sees it as a deliberate and malicious maneuver: if they want the place so badly, let them keep it; and he resigns as rector (not as a teacher). A one-vote victory; the vote reversed during a recess; a recruiting trip to Chicago refused. Consequences: Bill and Mary Caroline obtain a year's leave and leave the campus shortly afterward.

Dreier takes over the rectorship temporarily after Levi's resignation; some social science students leave at once, one of whom steals three or four books from the library, including Kenneth Burke's Permanence and Change. A stolen book: Kenneth Burke, Permanence and Change Consequences: The beginning of the fall in enrollment

At a faculty meeting, M.C. Richards presents a survey asking the students which fields should be added to the faculty. 16 for English; 13 for a second art teacher; 19 for social studies; 10 for psychology; first choices: 11 psychology, 3 social sciences, 5 art, 3 English Consequences: Justifies the humanities orientation M.C. advocates

Fuller arrives in June in a three-wheeled Dymaxion camper filled with models of energetic geometry; his optimism and exuberant personality immediately win converts. Three wheels; models of polyhedrons with circular hinges. Consequences: Fuller's most enthusiastic reception to date.

Fuller builds constructions with the silverware, helped by Elaine's bobby pins; Elaine's hamburger arrives, she refuses to take back her utensils and pulls a clip from her bag to hold her food; Fuller at once draws a lesson from it Words: Fuller: which brings us to the paradox of tensile strength! Atmosphere: A brilliant child's game, the waitress's involuntary comedy Stakes: Engineering invades daily life; Elaine's fascination

Bill wants to title a canvas “Interior”; Elaine sets an ultimatum: a specific room must be named; Bill answers “Attic, because you put everything in it”. Words: Bill: “Attic, because you put everything in it.” Atmosphere: Marital banter over titling. Stakes: Elaine's role as editor of Bill's work.

A silent refusal, with a look, of the 50-cent pillows; a night squirming on hard surfaces; detective novels read until dawn; at dawn, a dizzying climb up the mountain, a sumptuous green landscape. Words: A mute look: a dollar's worth of pillows would be an outrageous luxury Atmosphere: groggy but elated Stakes: Saving every dollar against comfort

A conversation on the dock, the bell, a general rush to the dining hall; they dawdle and arrive 20 minutes later: the hall cleaned out of every scrap. Words: Bill laughs: look at them run. Elaine, haughtily: “Pavlov's dogs” Atmosphere: hilarity, then a lesson Stakes: The illusion of the observer's superiority

The Levi camp wins a vote by one vote; during a recess or postponement, some of Levi's supporters leave the room; the vote is reconsidered and reversed; Levi sees it as a deliberate and malicious maneuver and resigns as rector. Words: Levi: if they wanted the place so badly, they could keep it. Atmosphere: Parliamentary tension, suspicion, a feeling of betrayal. Stakes: The tipping point of the Albers-Levi schism.

Fuller turns up in June in a three-wheeled camper stuffed with models of energetic geometry; by sheer force of his exuberant personality and mischievous enthusiasm, he immediately converts teachers and students. Words: He slips into his marathon lectures asides such as our dear friend the hypotenuse. Atmosphere: Energy, charm, unfailing optimism; Fuller's most enthusiastic reception to date. Stakes: The serial failure, a renegade, at last finds a public that embraces him.

10 p.m.: the porter offers pillows for rent, 50 cents apiece. Bill and Elaine look at each other: instant silent agreement — with 94 dollars for the whole summer, a dollar's worth of pillows would be a disproportionate luxury. The night drags on; wherever they turn their heads, hard surfaces and sharp corners. They give up on sleep and read detective novels all night. Words: No words: everything passes through an exchange of looks and a tacit agreement — material for actors Atmosphere: Stubborn cheerfulness, fatigue, the glow of reading, the rattle of the train Stakes: Money counted down to the pillow, a month before Black Mountain solves everything

At 10 p.m., the porter offers pillows at 50 cents; an exchanged look, a silent decision to refuse; the night drags on, hard surfaces and sharp corners; they give up on sleep and read detective novels until dawn, when the train climbs the mountain through a dazzling green landscape Atmosphere: groggy but elated at dawn Stakes: making $94 last the whole summer

On a rainy day, the class bolts together the aluminum strips; the dome rises only a few feet before collapsing; the Bauhaus types laugh like the onlookers at Fulton's steamboat, but Elaine is convinced that Fuller is right. 6 great circles of aluminum venetian-blind slats; planned height: 22 feet (about 6.70 m); the calculation required double strips, but the budget allowed single ones; christened the Supine Dome Consequences: Fuller will later claim he wanted to demonstrate the safety of a collapse

Cage stages Satie's play on an out-of-tune piano; Elaine plays Frisette, daughter of Baron Medusa; Fuller plays the baron; Cunningham dances a mechanical monkey between the scenes (sixty-second dances); Arthur Penn directs. William Schrager, the handsomest student on campus, plays Frisette's suitor

Within a fortnight, Droll is wearing sandals, has rolled his khakis up to the knee, and is beginning to follow the conversations — except when Fuller tells him, on a mountaintop one night, that by standing a certain way one can feel the earth turning: a relapse of culture shock. By the end of the summer he knows his life has changed. Sandals; khakis rolled to the knee; a night on a summit Consequences: Stays on as a full-time student the following year

After leaving the campus, the Levis stay with the Rondthalers in their house on Ocracoke, a preliminary to their departure for Europe. From there, M.C. writes the Dreiers a long, brutally frank letter summing up her resentment of the Albers putsch. Consequences: The letter formalizes the ideological break between the two camps.

About twenty rotating teachers in the July-August session, with Albers, Cage, Cunningham, Fuller, and de Kooning at the core, joined by about 75 students in painting, sculpture, and theater. About 20 teachers, about 75 students; Ray Johnson speaks of a “galaxy of talent”

The three men have breakfast together every day; they dream up a whimsical “finishing school”: “We would finish anything” — abolishing all conventional approaches to school. Consequences: A lifelong friendship between Cage and Fuller, born of their shared embrace of unforeseen results

De Kooning made drawings in the living room; Elaine: “He was in a vacuum that he began to fill with pastels”; he worked feverishly for a few weeks until the walls were covered with pastels, then fixed a 25 × 32-inch sheet of paper to an easel and moved on to oil: Asheville was being born. pastels covering the walls; a 25 × 32-inch sheet (the actual work: cardboard, enamel, ~26 × 32 inches) Consequences: Asheville (1948), the first manifestation of his mature style on a small scale.
De Kooning scraped and rebuilt rather than piling up; Elaine reports the painful experience of coming in and finding a beloved image “blasted away”. a thin surface, scraped and rebuilt
Willem worked in the cottage, but the couple were separated, and Willem often slept elsewhere (Stevens and Swan).

A Pratt graduate in 1948, Ray saw the small ad in The Nation announcing Mark Tobey for the summer and took the train. The passengers got off along the way; left alone, he went over to the two men at the back: Cage and Cunningham. Cage told him that Tobey was ill and had been replaced by de Kooning. A small ad in The Nation; a beautiful train ride; an almost empty car Consequences: Ray arrives at BMC for the summer of 1948

About seventy-five students in painting, sculpture, and theater, including Ruth Asawa, Joseph Fiore, Betty and Peter Jennerhahn, Ray Johnson, Hazel Larsen Archer, Kenneth Noland, Arthur Penn, Kenneth Snelson, Paul and Vera Williams. about 75 students Consequences: Paul and Vera Williams will support Cage and Cunningham financially; Williams Mix (1952-53) will bear their name

During the summer at Black Mountain, news arrives of Arshile Gorky's suicide. De Kooning, protective of his friend's spirit, refuses any tearful analysis. De Kooning's reaction: Gorky was a peasant; he was very strong, so when his body betrayed him, he got rid of it. Consequences: De Kooning then writes a letter to ARTnews about Gorky.

His neck broken in a car accident, his painting arm temporarily paralyzed; three weeks later, after warning almost everyone he met, he hangs himself. He openly announced his intention Consequences: Shock in the New York milieu

Albers animatedly describes the construction of each building. A visit to the Quiet House, a place of meditation built by a student in memory of another student killed in a car accident, Ted Dreier's son. A long building of tiny Bauhaus-style studios; Bill refuses to paint there and chooses the cottage's living room; Elaine pushes her desk against the window overlooking the lake and paints on kraft paper pinned to the wall. studios with a narrow cot, a sturdy desk, a chair; a dock in the distance, students diving in the sun Consequences: The two studios set up
